lesson_title: The Queue of 100: SA's World Record Nobody Wants
hook_text: Line up 100 South Africans and count the money. By person 60... you've counted 10 coins.
clip_script: Line up one hundred people, arranged from the emptiest pockets on the left to the fullest on the right. All the income earned this year is one hundred coins. If sharing were perfectly equal, every step adds exactly one coin. Now count the real South African queue. Walk past the first twenty people and your count reaches barely two or three coins. Keep going to person sixty and you have only around ten coins, though you have passed more than half the country. Then the count explodes: the last ten people are holding roughly sixty-five of the hundred coins between them. That sag is the Lorenz curve, and its number — the Gini — puts South Africa at zero comma six three: the deepest sag of any major economy on Earth.
visual_style: An overhead queue of 100 figures with a running coin counter that crawls, crawls, then avalanches over the final ten figures.
mood: Quietly stunning — let the numbers do the shouting.
pacing: Slow deliberate counting that suddenly accelerates into the avalanche, ending on the world-record line.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson: the Lorenz curve, the Gini, and what redistribution can actually do.
